title: Materials Around Us
description: Grade 1 Science: the materials all around us — wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper and cloth. Their properties and uses, float or sink, natural or man-made, with games.

topics.title: Everything Is Made of Materials
topics.concept:
Everything around us is made from something. That something is called a material. Here are some common materials:

  • 🪵 Wood — from trees (chairs, tables, pencils).
  • 🔩 Metal — strong and shiny (spoons, keys, cars).
  • 🥤 Plastic — light and bendy (bottles, toys, buckets).
  • 🪟 Glass — clear and breakable (windows, tumblers).
  • 📄 Paper — thin and light (books, notebooks).
  • 🧵 Cloth — soft (clothes, towels).

recap: Common materials: wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper, cloth.
We pick a material to suit the job.

wonder.text: Look around your room. Your chair, your cup, your clothes — what is each one made of?

qa.q: Can one thing be made of many materials?
qa.a: Yes! A pencil has wood on the outside, a metal band, and a rubber eraser. Many everyday things use more than one material.

qa.q: Why isn't a window made of wood?
qa.a: We choose materials by their job. A window is glass because glass is clear and lets us see through it — wood would block the view!

topics.title: Hard or Soft, Rough or Smooth
topics.concept:
Materials have properties — words that describe what they are like:

  • 🪨 Hard — does not press in (rock, metal). Soft — presses in easily (pillow, cotton).
  • 🧱 Rough — bumpy to touch (brick, sandpaper). Smooth — flat and slippery (glass, ice).
  • ✨ Shiny — reflects light (metal, mirror). Dull — does not shine (wood, paper).
topics.visual: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 155" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="320" height="155" fill="#fff"/><rect x="10" y="14" width="146" height="124" rx="14" fill="#e6e8ee"/><text x="50" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🪨</text><text x="106" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🥄</text><text x="83" y="120" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#23314f" text-anchor="middle">Hard</text><rect x="164" y="14" width="146" height="124" rx="14" fill="#fdeef0"/><text x="204" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🛏️</text><text x="260" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🧸</text><text x="237" y="120" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#23314f" text-anchor="middle">Soft</text></svg>
recap: Properties describe what a material is like.
Hard / soft, rough / smooth, shiny / dull.
We choose properties to suit the job (soft pillow, hard table).

wonder.text: Press a rock, then press a pillow. They feel so different! Why?

qa.a: Glass is hard and smooth — but also breakable! That is why we hold glass things carefully.
Soft materials like cotton press in gently, so they are comfy to rest your head on. A hard pillow would not be nice to sleep on!

topics.title: Materials and Their Uses
topics.concept:
We choose a material because of what it can do:

  • 🪵 Wood is strong → chairs, tables, doors.
  • 🪟 Glass is clear → windows, spectacles.
  • 🥤 Plastic is waterproof → raincoats, buckets, bottles.
  • 🧵 Cloth is soft → clothes, blankets.
  • 📄 Paper is light → books, notebooks.

recap: We choose a material for its special job.
Wood → furniture, glass → windows, plastic → waterproof things.

wonder.text: Why do we make raincoats from plastic and not from paper?

qa.q: Why not make a raincoat from paper?
qa.a: Paper soaks up water and falls apart when wet. Plastic keeps water out, so it keeps you dry — perfect for a raincoat!

qa.q: Why are cooking pots made of metal?
qa.a: Metal is strong and does not melt or burn on a hot stove. It also carries heat well to cook the food. Plastic would melt!

topics.title: Float or Sink
topics.concept:
When we put things in water, some float (stay on top) and some sink (go down).

  • 🛟 Float — leaf, cork, plastic boat, wood.
  • ⬇️ Sink — coin, stone, key, metal spoon.

Heavy, solid things often sink, while light things and things with trapped air often float. The best way to know is to test it!
topics.visual: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 155" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="320" height="155" fill="#eef6ff"/><rect x="10" y="14" width="146" height="124" rx="14" fill="#d8f0ff"/><text x="50" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🍃</text><text x="106" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">⛵</text><text x="83" y="120" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#23314f" text-anchor="middle">Floats</text><rect x="164" y="14" width="146" height="124" rx="14" fill="#e6e8ee"/><text x="204" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🪙</text><text x="260" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🪨</text><text x="237" y="120" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#23314f" text-anchor="middle">Sinks</text></svg>
recap: Some things float (stay on top); some sink (go down).
Light things and trapped air help things float.
The best way to know is to test it in water.

wonder.text: Drop a coin in water — it sinks. Drop a leaf — it floats. Can you guess why?

qa.q: How does a heavy metal ship float?
qa.a: A ship is shaped like a big hollow bowl full of air. That clever shape spreads its weight and traps air, so the whole ship floats — even though metal alone sinks!

qa.q: Will the same thing always float?
qa.a: Usually yes — but if it fills up with water (like a cup with holes), it can sink. Scientists always test to be sure.

topics.title: Natural or Made by People
topics.concept:
Materials come from two places:

  • 🌿 Natural — found in nature: wood (from trees), cotton (from plants), stone, water, wool (from sheep).
  • 🏭 Made by people (man-made) — made in factories: plastic, glass and paper.

Some man-made materials still start from natural things — paper is made from wood, and glass is made from sand!
topics.visual: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 155" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="320" height="155" fill="#fff"/><rect x="10" y="14" width="146" height="124" rx="14" fill="#e6f3d8"/><text x="50" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🪵</text><text x="106" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🌿</text><text x="83" y="120" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#23314f" text-anchor="middle">Natural</text><rect x="164" y="14" width="146" height="124" rx="14" fill="#eae6ff"/><text x="204" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🥤</text><text x="260" y="78" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🪟</text><text x="237" y="120" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#23314f" text-anchor="middle">Made by people</text></svg>
recap: Natural materials come from nature (wood, cotton, stone).
Man-made materials are made in factories (plastic, glass).
Some man-made things start from natural ones (paper from wood).

wonder.text: Wood comes from trees. But where does a plastic toy come from?

qa.a: Cotton is natural — it grows on the cotton plant. People then spin it into thread and weave it into cloth for our clothes.

qa.q: Paper is made by people, so why is it from a tree?
qa.a: Good thinking! Paper is man-made in a factory, but the factory uses wood from trees to make it. That is why we should not waste paper — it saves trees.

questions.explanation: A window is made of glass so we can see through it.
A pillow is soft — it presses in gently.

questions.q: Which material is waterproof and good for a raincoat?
questions.explanation: Plastic keeps water out, so it is great for raincoats.

questions.q: Which of these will SINK in water?
questions.explanation: A coin is small, heavy and solid, so it sinks.
Wood is natural — it comes from trees.

questions.q: A spoon is usually made of…
questions.explanation: Spoons are made of metal — strong and easy to clean.

questions.q: Why is a cooking pot made of metal and not plastic?
options: Plastic would melt on the heat
questions.explanation: Metal does not melt on a hot stove, but plastic would melt.

questions.q: How does a heavy metal ship float?
questions.explanation: A ship's hollow, bowl-like shape traps air and spreads its weight, so it floats.

questions.q: Paper is made by people, but it starts from…
questions.explanation: Paper is made in factories from the wood of trees — so we should not waste it.

questions.q: Which set lists only NATURAL materials?
questions.explanation: Wood, cotton and stone all come from nature.

questions.q: A pencil is made of more than one material. Which is the writing tip usually made from?
questions.explanation: A pencil's tip is graphite, wrapped in wood — more than one material in one object.
